title: Simulacro 09 — Kubernetes, service mesh y patrones cloud-native
focus: Kubernetes patterns (init containers, sidecars, ambassador, operator), service mesh (Istio/Linkerd), stateful vs stateless, StatefulSets, node affinity, cost of over-provisioning y por qué 'todo en K8s' no siempre es la respuesta.

questions.scenario: Necesitas añadir mTLS, retries, y observability a 50 microservicios escritos en 4 lenguajes diferentes (Go, Python, Java, Node). Dev leader propone escribir librería en cada language.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es el approach cloud-native canónico y por qué?

options.text: Sidecar pattern: cada Pod incluye un container adicional (sidecar) que maneja cross-cutting concerns (mTLS, retries, tracing, metrics) transparentemente. La app habla localhost al sidecar, sidecar habla al network. Language-agnostic. Envoy es el sidecar canónico usado por Istio, Linkerd (linkerd-proxy), Consul Connect. Actualizar comportamiento no requiere tocar app code.
options.why: Correcto. Sidecar (Netflix Prana era el original, Envoy es el estándar actual) resuelve exactly este problema: cross-cutting concerns implementados una vez, deployed junto a cualquier app, transparently. Beneficios: (1) Language-agnostic (funciona igual con Python, Go, Java). (2) Ops team owns sidecar (security, TLS certs, retries) — app team focus on business logic. (3) Update sidecar without touching app code. Trade-offs: (a) Overhead — extra container per pod (memoria, CPU, ~50-100MB Envoy typical). (b) Latency — one extra hop localhost (usually <1ms). (c) Complexity — sidecar injection, lifecycle management. Servicemesh (Istio, Linkerd) automatiza inyección + control plane.

options.text: Escribir librería en cada language — código explícito es mejor.
options.why: Coste massivo: 4x duplicación, cada actualización requires 4 changes + coordinated release. Bugs asimétricos entre languages. No escala. Sidecar elimina esta duplicación.

options.text: Reescribir todo en un lenguaje único.
options.why: Migrar 50 servicios a un lenguaje es proyecto multi-año que no resuelve el problema de fondo. Además nuevo language también needs library. Sidecar es abstraction correcta.

options.text: API Gateway central que maneja mTLS, retries.
options.why: API Gateway es north-south (external → internal). Sidecar es east-west (service → service). Diferentes problemas. Gateway no cubre service-to-service en muchos casos, y crea SPOF/bottleneck para internal traffic.

questions.explanation: Sidecar pattern (Bilgin Ibryam popularizó el término) is one of Kubernetes' most impactful patterns. Setup: Pod has main container (app) + sidecar container (Envoy/proxy). Kubernetes co-schedules them (same node, share network namespace). App talks to localhost:port; sidecar handles rest. Common sidecar use cases: (1) Service mesh proxy (Envoy in Istio, linkerd-proxy in Linkerd). (2) Logging (Fluent Bit sidecar tails app logs → sends to central). (3) Config reload (Consul-template sidecar watches for changes, reloads). (4) TLS termination. (5) Metrics collection. (6) Vault agent sidecar for secrets rotation. Considerations: (a) Resource overhead — 50-100MB memory per Pod for Envoy typical. In cluster with 1000 pods = ~50-100GB. Not trivial. (b) Startup ordering — init container to configure, then main + sidecar concurrent (Kubernetes 1.29 native sidecar support with startup ordering). (c) Injection — mutating admission webhook auto-inject sidecar (Istio, Linkerd automate). Alternative: ambient mesh (Istio 2023+) removes sidecar per pod, uses node-level proxy — reduces overhead, more complex operationally.
questions.realWorld: Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect use sidecar universally. Netflix Envoy pioneered cloud-native sidecar. Uber Sidecar (before Envoy) for RPC. Airbnb SmartStack (older) similar concept. Ambient mesh (Istio 2023+) is response to sidecar overhead in huge clusters — moves shared functions to per-node proxy. Trade-offs still debated: sidecar (isolated, simpler mental model) vs ambient (efficient, complex).

questions.scenario: App container requiere que la DB migration se ejecute antes de arrancar, o que un secret se obtenga de Vault, o que un config file se descargue. Dev quiere hacerlo en el entrypoint de la app.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es el pattern Kubernetes-native?

options.text: Init containers: containers que corren SECUENCIALMENTE antes de que main containers arranquen. Cada init container debe complete successfully para que el pod prosiga. Uso: DB migrations, config download, secret fetching, wait-for-dependencies, permissions setup. Separan concerns: main container focus on runtime, init handle bootstrap.
options.why: Correcto. Init containers son first-class citizen en Kubernetes desde ~2016 (v1.3). Beneficios: (1) Separación de concerns — bootstrap logic apart from app logic. (2) Different images — init puede usar image con curl/kubectl mientras main es distroless. (3) Reuse — misma init logic en múltiples deployments. (4) Failure semantics — init failure prevents main start (fail fast). (5) Sequential execution — orden garantizado init1 → init2 → main. Trade-off: extra pod startup time (init containers add seconds).

options.text: Hacer todo en el entrypoint del main container.
options.why: Mezcla bootstrap con runtime. Main container image bloated con tooling (curl, kubectl) que solo se necesita en start. Failure semantics unclear (¿qué exit code significa migration failed vs app crashed?).

options.text: Job separado que corre antes del deployment.
options.why: Válido para algunos casos (one-time migrations) pero coordination difícil (¿cómo el deployment sabe que el job completó? ArgoCD sync waves). Init containers son coupled con Pod lifecycle, más idiomatic para per-pod bootstrap.

options.text: Hook 'preStart' del container.
options.why: Kubernetes NO tiene preStart hook (tiene postStart which runs concurrent, not blocking). Init containers son el mecanismo canónico.

questions.explanation: Init containers: (1) Run to completion sequentially before main containers start. (2) Full container images (any language, any tooling). (3) Failure blocks Pod from progressing. (4) Restarts on failure (per restartPolicy). Common patterns: (a) Wait-for-dependency: init container polls DB/API/service and blocks until ready. `until pg_isready; do sleep 1; done`. (b) Database migrations: `rails db:migrate` or `flyway migrate`. (c) Secret bootstrapping: fetch from Vault, write to shared volume (main container reads). (d) Config generation: `envsubst` template → shared volume. (e) Permissions setup: `chown -R user:group /data` on volumes. (f) Downloading assets/models: for ML pods, download model weights. Kubernetes 1.29+ has 'native sidecar' feature (restartPolicy: Always in init container list) — sidecar starts before main and stays running. Distinguish from postStart hook (runs after container start, non-blocking, no ordering guarantee).
questions.realWorld: Every serious Kubernetes deployment uses init containers. Common: (1) Cert-manager waits for cert-manager CRDs via init. (2) Vault Agent injects secrets via init + sidecar combo. (3) Istio uses init container for iptables rules setup (before ambient mode). (4) DB migrations for Rails/Django deployments. (5) Elasticsearch operator uses init for permissions on data volumes. Sin init containers, bootstrap logic bloats main containers y confuses lifecycle.

questions.scenario: App legacy no soporta service discovery moderna (habla a hardcoded hostnames). Necesitas que use nuevos backend endpoints dinámicos sin modificar código.
questions.question: ¿Cuál pattern Kubernetes ayuda?

options.text: Ambassador pattern: sidecar container que actúa como proxy/adapter local. App habla localhost al ambassador; ambassador habla al backend real (service discovery, load balancing, retries). Adaptación a legacy app sin cambiar código. Similar al sidecar service mesh pero focused en adaptar external world para la app.
options.why: Correcto. Ambassador (Netflix Prana, extendido por Bilgin Ibryam) es specialized sidecar for adapting/proxying external services. Use case: legacy app hardcoded to 'db-server:5432' — deploy ambassador that listens on localhost:5432, proxies to actual DB (which may be in different service, cluster, cloud). Similar functionality: service mesh sidecar (Envoy), but ambassador is more targeted to specific adaptations (protocol translation, connection pooling, encryption). Trade-off: extra container overhead.

options.text: Modificar la app para usar Kubernetes service discovery.
options.why: Válido pero costoso si legacy con múltiples deployments, o si can't modify code (vendor, compliance). Ambassador es solución cuando modification is impractical.

options.text: DNS rewrite via CoreDNS.
options.why: Válido para simple rewrites (hostname A → hostname B) pero limited: no protocol translation, no load balancing logic, no connection pooling. Ambassador es más general.

options.text: iptables rules para NAT.
options.why: Muy low-level, difícil de mantener, poco flexible. Ambassador es abstraction correcta a nivel Kubernetes.

questions.explanation: Ambassador pattern: (1) Sidecar container acting as proxy for outbound traffic from main app. (2) App connects to localhost:port. (3) Ambassador handles the 'real world': service discovery, LB, retries, circuit breaking, protocol translation, encryption. (4) Similar to service mesh sidecar but often more targeted / language-specific. Use cases: (a) Legacy app modernization — old app to new backends without code change. (b) Protocol translation — app speaks HTTP, backend requires gRPC. Ambassador translates. (c) Client library replacement — instead of updating client library in N languages, ambassador provides consistent behavior. (d) Multi-region routing — ambassador routes to closest region. (e) Cross-cluster bridging — app in cluster A talks to service in cluster B via ambassador. Distinction from other patterns: (a) Sidecar (general) — any cross-cutting concern (logging, config). (b) Ambassador — specifically proxying outbound. (c) Adapter — different: standardizes app OUTPUT (metrics, logs) for external consumption. Netflix Prana was original ambassador; Envoy/Linkerd sidecars often serve ambassador role in mesh contexts.
questions.realWorld: Netflix Prana bridged Java services to their Eureka discovery. Airbnb Nerve/Synapse similar. Envoy is used as ambassador in many settings. Cloud provider service adapters (e.g., AWS Ambassador in some architectures) proxy to cloud APIs. Vault Agent as ambassador serves credentials to apps that can't natively integrate Vault.

questions.scenario: Deploy y operar Postgres HA cluster en Kubernetes requiere: init primary, add replicas, monitor, failover, backups, rolling upgrades, PVC management. Team pregunta: ¿Helm chart o Operator?
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la diferencia y cuándo elegir cada uno?

options.text: Helm chart: package de templates YAML + values. Instala/upgrade recursos declarativamente. Bueno para stateless apps + config templating. Limitación: no encapsula operational knowledge de day-2 ops (failover, backup, monitoring). Operator: custom controller que watch custom resources (CRDs) y ejecuta operational logic. Encapsula 'human operator knowledge' as code. Bueno para stateful/complex apps donde day-2 ops matter. Postgres, Elasticsearch, Kafka tienen operators mature.
options.why: Correcto. Distinction crucial. Helm es TEMPLATE ENGINE — good para: standard deployments, config variations, one-shot install/upgrade. Operator es CONTROLLER — watches CRDs, reacts continuously, implements domain-specific ops (Postgres cluster: monitor primary health, elect new primary on failure, add replicas, PITR restore). Operator pattern (CoreOS 2016) codifies operational expertise. For complex stateful services, operator strongly preferred: Zalando Postgres Operator, Elastic Cloud on K8s, Strimzi Kafka, cert-manager. Simple stateless apps: Helm sufficient.

options.text: Helm siempre — es más simple.
options.why: Simplicity trade-off: Helm doesn't handle day-2 ops. Deploying Postgres via Helm is easy; managing failover, backups, upgrades is manual. Operator automates this. Complex stateful services benefit substantially.

options.text: Operator siempre — más powerful.
options.why: Operators son more complex to develop y mantener. For simple stateless apps (web servers, batch jobs), Helm es sufficient y avoids operator overhead. Elegir según complexity.

options.text: Son lo mismo — diferentes nombres.
options.why: Fundamentally different. Helm es templating tool (client-side render); Operator es controller (running in cluster, reacting to events).

questions.explanation: Kubernetes Operator pattern (CoreOS 2016): (1) Define CRD (Custom Resource Definition) representing domain concept ('PostgresCluster', 'ElasticsearchCluster'). (2) Deploy controller (Operator) that watches CRD instances. (3) Controller reconciles desired state (CRD spec) to actual (cluster status). (4) Implements complex operational logic: init, scale, backup, upgrade, failover, monitoring. Benefits: (a) Encapsulates expertise — DBA/SRE knowledge as code. (b) Consistent ops — automated failover, backups. (c) Declarative — user says 'want Postgres 15 HA with 3 nodes and backups every 6h', operator handles rest. (d) Extensible — organizations write custom operators. Tools: Operator SDK, Kubebuilder for building. Framework: Golang typical. Notable operators: cert-manager (TLS certs), Prometheus Operator, Strimzi (Kafka), Elastic Operator, Zalando Postgres Operator, Crunchy Postgres Operator, CloudNativePG. Helm complementary: many operators installed via Helm chart initially. Helm for one-shot config, Operator for continuous management.
questions.realWorld: Every serious stateful workload on Kubernetes runs via operator: Elasticsearch on K8s (ECK), Kafka via Strimzi, Postgres via Zalando/CNPG, Redis via Redis Operator, cert-manager for TLS. GitHub Actions Runner Controller is operator. Prometheus/Grafana ecosystem uses operators. CNCF landscape has 100+ operators. Building custom operators for internal platforms is common at large orgs.

questions.scenario: Necesitas deployar Postgres primary + 2 replicas en Kubernetes. Team pregunta: ¿Deployment o StatefulSet?
questions.question: ¿Cuál es apropiado y por qué?

options.text: StatefulSet: Pods tienen identidad estable (nombre postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2), orden de deployment/rollout predictable, PersistentVolumeClaims por pod (persistent y estables), DNS names estables. Diseñado para stateful services (DBs, queues, distributed systems) que requieren identidad y storage estable. Deployment: sin identidad estable (random hash names), sin ordering guarantees, sin PVC per replica. Bueno para stateless services (web, API).
options.why: Correcto. StatefulSet características: (1) Nombres estables (postgres-0, postgres-1). (2) DNS estable (postgres-0.postgres.default.svc). (3) PVC per pod, remains when pod recreated. (4) Ordered rollout (0 first, then 1, then 2). (5) Ordered scaling down (reverse: 2, 1, 0). Estas properties matter para stateful services: replica knows its role by name, storage persists across restarts, replication set config stable. Deployment features (random names, parallel rollout) work fine for stateless pero fail for stateful (replica identifiers change, storage lost).

options.text: Deployment con volume mount es sufficient.
options.why: Falso para stateful: (1) Deployment pods have random names — replica config can't reference stable names. (2) Storage: Deployment con PVC comparte el PVC entre replicas (o requiere hack); StatefulSet gives each replica its own PVC. (3) Ordering: Deployment scales up/down all at once, breaking cluster (Postgres needs primary before replicas).

options.text: DaemonSet — un Postgres por nodo.
options.why: DaemonSet is for 'one pod per node' patterns (log collectors, monitoring agents). Postgres cluster doesn't want pod-per-node semantics — wants N replicas regardless of node count.

options.text: Job — Postgres es workload que corre y termina.
options.why: Job es para one-shot workloads (batch, migrations). Postgres runs continuously. Wrong workload type.

questions.explanation: Workload types en Kubernetes: (1) Deployment — stateless, rollout via rolling ReplicaSet updates, random pod names, parallel scaling. Web servers, APIs. (2) StatefulSet — stateful, stable identities, ordered ops, per-pod PVC. DBs, queues, distributed systems (Cassandra, ETCD, Kafka). (3) DaemonSet — one pod per node (or matching node selector). Log collectors, monitoring agents, kube-proxy. (4) Job — run to completion, retry on failure. Batch, migrations. (5) CronJob — scheduled Jobs. StatefulSet details: (a) Pod names: `<sts-name>-0`, `<sts-name>-1`, etc. Stable across recreation. (b) DNS: through headless Service, `<pod-name>.<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. (c) VolumeClaimTemplates create separate PVC per pod. (d) Rolling update reverses (last to first). Considerations: (a) Stateful workloads on K8s traditionally complex — many recommend operators (Zalando, CNPG) instead of raw StatefulSet. (b) Pod disruption budgets essential to prevent losing quorum. (c) Persistent storage class (SSD/local) affects performance. (d) Debate ongoing: run stateful on K8s or use managed service (RDS, Aurora)? Both valid depending on needs.
questions.realWorld: Cassandra, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, ETCD all use StatefulSets when self-hosted on K8s. Operators wrap StatefulSet with domain-specific logic. Airbnb famously wrote about running stateful on K8s. Slack, Uber run large stateful workloads. Managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL, Cosmos DB) alternative — avoid K8s complexity for critical DBs. Trade-off: control (K8s) vs simplicity (managed).

questions.scenario: Startup con 8 microservicios en Kubernetes evalúa Istio para 'best practices'. VP Engineering pregunta si vale la pena la complejidad.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la respuesta correcta?

options.text: Sí, Istio siempre — es el standard cloud-native.
options.why: Simplistic. Istio adds significant complexity (control plane, sidecar injection, mTLS certs, config CRDs). Con 8 servicios sencillos, ROI puede ser negativo — más operational load que value delivered.

options.text: Depende: service mesh justifica cuando (a) MUCHOS servicios (>20+) requiring uniform policy; (b) heterogeneous languages (implement retries/mTLS N times painful); (c) fine-grained authz/routing (canary deploy, A/B, traffic mirroring); (d) compliance requiring mTLS everywhere. Para <20 services, simple Ingress + language-native libs (Resilience4j, Polly) es más simple. Linkerd (más liviano) es alternativa a Istio (más completo pero pesado). Ambient mesh (Istio 2023+) reduces overhead — worth evaluating.
options.why: Correcto y matizado. Service mesh es powerful pero costoso operacionalmente. Value scales with #services + heterogeneity. Small orgs con few services should defer. Linkerd is a lighter alternative (simpler, less feature-rich); Istio is full-featured pero complex. Ambient mesh (Istio 2023+) reduces sidecar overhead. Decision criteria: uniform policy needs, compliance, service count, team maturity. VP should evaluate concrete needs, not blanket adopt.

options.text: No, service mesh es siempre over-engineering.
options.why: Otro extremo. Para orgs con 100+ services in heterogeneous languages, service mesh delivers massive value (uniform mTLS, observability, policies). Google's Anthos, Microsoft's platform, Uber all use service mesh at scale.

options.text: Depende del budget: Istio si tienes presupuesto, si no Linkerd.
options.why: Ambos are open-source (free). El costo no es licencia, es COMPLEXIDAD OPERACIONAL. Cost es engineering time to maintain. Decision by complexity fit, not budget.

questions.explanation: Service mesh trade-offs: Value: (a) mTLS everywhere without app changes. (b) Uniform retries, circuit breakers, timeouts. (c) Advanced traffic routing (canary, A/B, mirror). (d) Observability (traces, metrics per service call). (e) Authorization policies. Cost: (a) Control plane operational overhead (Istio's istiod, config CRDs). (b) Sidecar resource overhead (Envoy ~50-100MB/pod). (c) Latency (extra hop). (d) Learning curve (Istio config is complex — VirtualService, DestinationRule, PeerAuthentication). (e) Debugging complexity (add mesh to traces). Options 2026: (1) Istio — full-featured, sidecar (or ambient 2023+), CNCF graduate. (2) Linkerd — simpler, lighter, sidecar-only, CNCF graduate. (3) Consul Connect — HashiCorp stack. (4) AWS App Mesh — managed. (5) Cilium Service Mesh — eBPF-based, sidecar-less. Decision framework: start without mesh; add when uniform policy needed at scale. Google/Microsoft/Amazon all use mesh at their scale. Small orgs frequently don't need it. Ambient mesh reducing overhead may shift ROI.
questions.realWorld: Uber, Slack, Airbnb use service mesh at scale. Google's Anthos (managed Istio). Microsoft's Open Service Mesh. Netflix has custom (Zuul, Ribbon originally). Kubernetes SIG produced Gateway API standardizing traffic management. Ambient mesh (Istio) 2023+ addresses sidecar overhead concerns. Debate 'do you need service mesh?' ongoing in cloud-native community.

references.title: William Morgan — 'Do you need a service mesh?'

questions.scenario: Deployment de 3 replicas debe distribuirse across 3 nodes for HA (si un node cae, 2 replicas sobreviven). Además pods DB tienen que estar en nodos con SSD.
questions.question: ¿Qué mecanismos Kubernetes ayudan?

options.text: PodAntiAffinity con topologyKey=kubernetes.io/hostname: evita que 2 replicas se schedule en el mismo node. Distribution garantizada across nodes (dentro de disponibilidad).
options.why: Correcto. PodAntiAffinity spec le dice a scheduler 'don't schedule these pods on same node/zone/region'. RequiredDuringScheduling means hard requirement (mejor no arrancar que violar); PreferredDuringScheduling es soft (best-effort). Común pattern: hard anti-affinity by hostname. Para multi-zone HA: preferred anti-affinity by zone.

options.text: NodeAffinity con requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution y matchExpressions node label 'disktype=ssd': schedule pod solo en nodes labeled ssd.
options.why: Correcto. NodeAffinity is más expressive que nodeSelector (soporta operators In, NotIn, Exists, Gt, Lt). Required = hard constraint. Ignored during execution = won't evict if label changes post-schedule. Common patterns: schedule GPU pods on GPU nodes, DB pods on high-IO nodes, batch on spot instances.

options.text: TopologySpreadConstraints: distribuir uniformly across topology domains (zones, nodes, regions). Más declarative y flexible que anti-affinity para skew control.
options.why: Correcto. TopologySpreadConstraints (Kubernetes 1.18+) supersedes many uses of anti-affinity. Declara maxSkew (allowed imbalance) + topology (zone, node). Scheduler places to minimize skew. Better than anti-affinity for balance-focused (vs strict separation). Cloud providers use this for zone spread.

options.text: Taints y tolerations para dedicar nodos a workloads.
options.why: Taints/tolerations son mecanismo distinto: taints repel pods from nodes UNLESS pod tolerates. Uso para dedicar nodos (GPUs, spot, sensitive). No directly answers 'distribute + place on ssd' pero complementary. Otras opciones son más directas.

options.text: Manual scheduling — deploy each replica to specific node.
options.why: Anti-Kubernetes philosophy. Manual scheduling defeats scheduler intelligence. Anti-affinity/topology constraints let scheduler decide dynamically as nodes come/go.

questions.explanation: Kubernetes scheduling primitives: (1) NodeSelector — simple label matching. `nodeSelector: {disktype: ssd}`. Basic. (2) NodeAffinity — expressive, supports In/NotIn/Gt/Lt/Exists. Required or Preferred. Applied to pod. (3) PodAffinity/AntiAffinity — schedule pod near/away from other pods matching selector. topologyKey defines granularity (hostname, zone, region). (4) TopologySpreadConstraints — declarative even distribution across topology. maxSkew parameter. (5) Taints/Tolerations — nodes taint themselves (kubectl taint nodes node1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule). Only pods with matching toleration can schedule. Uso: dedicate nodes to specific workloads. (6) Priority/preemption — high priority pods can preempt lower priority. (7) Custom schedulers — pluggable for advanced patterns (batch/ML orchestrators). Combinaciones: DB pods often use NodeAffinity(ssd) + PodAntiAffinity(hostname) + TopologySpread(zone). Balance HA + performance + cost. Common mistake: required anti-affinity que impide scheduling cuando insufficient nodes.
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes production at scale uses these extensively. Netflix, Airbnb, Uber have custom scheduling for GPU jobs, ML pipelines. Databricks uses spot node pools with taints. Karpenter (AWS) auto-provisions nodes matching affinity. Descheduler periodically re-balances if constraints violated after scheduling. Sin proper scheduling constraints, un cloud AZ outage tumba todos los replicas simultaneously.

questions.scenario: Debate en el team: 'Should we set CPU limits on our pods? Some sources say yes (predictability), otros no (throttling harms performance)'.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la práctica ACTUAL recomendada y por qué?

options.text: SIEMPRE set CPU limits — es la best practice de siempre.
options.why: Consensus MODERNO (Tim Hockin y otros SIG-Node) reconsidered: CPU limits cause throttling (CFS bandwidth control) even when free CPU available on node. Latency spikes. Many recommend: set REQUESTS correctly (guarantees minimum) but not LIMITS on CPU. Memory limits YES (uncontrolled memory = OOM cascade). Nuanced position.

options.text: Set MEMORY limits (mandatory) pero NO CPU limits (typically). Rationale: (1) Memory sin limit puede consume all node RAM → OOM kill de otros pods; (2) CPU limits cause CFS throttling under load even with idle CPU on node — latency spikes. Set CPU REQUESTS correctly for scheduling (guaranteed slice) + let pod burst if unused CPU available. Kubernetes SIG-Node y many cloud experts recomiendan esta configuration en 2024-2026.
options.why: Correcto. Position modern: (a) Memory limits: essential. Pod exceeding OOM killed. Sin limits, memory-hungry pod puede tumbar node entero. (b) CPU limits: controversial. CFS throttling with limits causes latency spikes even when node has idle CPU (bug/quirk of Linux CFS). Better: set requests (scheduling guarantee) + no limit, allowing burst. Google SREs, Kubernetes maintainers (Tim Hockin) publicaron sobre esto. Nuance: for multi-tenant clusters with SLA per tenant, CPU limits may still be needed. For internal/homogenous clusters, no CPU limits preferred.

options.text: Never set limits — Kubernetes will manage.
options.why: Falso for memory. Sin memory limits, memory leak in one pod OOM-kills entire node, affecting all pods on it. Memory limits essential for isolation.

options.text: Set both to same value as requests (Guaranteed QoS).
options.why: QoS Guaranteed (requests==limits) gives highest priority but con CPU limits causes throttling issues. Además wastes resources — Guaranteed pod can't burst. Only necessary for critical workloads que need guaranteed non-preemption.

questions.explanation: Requests vs Limits: (1) Requests — guaranteed resources scheduler considers for placement. Node allocatable divided among requests. (2) Limits — cap on usage. Enforced by kernel (memory via cgroups, CPU via CFS). Memory limits: hard enforce. Pod at limit → OOM kill. Essential to prevent runaway pod. CPU limits: throttled by CFS. Even if node has idle CPU, pod throttled to limit. Causes p99 latency spikes. Debated: for many workloads, no CPU limit + accurate requests is better. QoS classes (based on requests/limits): (a) Guaranteed — requests==limits for all resources. Never preempted, last to be evicted. (b) Burstable — some requests<limits. Can burst, preemptable. (c) BestEffort — no requests/limits. Preemptible first. Kubernetes SIG-Node discussion 2020+ shifted away from 'always set CPU limits'. Google SRE book (Ch. 21) mentions similar. Complications: (a) Multi-tenant clusters may need CPU limits for fair sharing (noisy neighbor). (b) Cost — no CPU limits + shared node = risk of noisy neighbor from other tenants (mitigated by dedicated node pools). (c) Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) can tune requests dynamically.
questions.realWorld: Grafana Labs, Datadog, Zalando publicaron sobre removing CPU limits improving latency. Google GKE docs discuss. Netflix uses accurate requests without CPU limits internally. AWS EKS best practices evolved similar. Debate ongoing but consensus shifting. Memory limits universally recommended. Watch cluster CPU throttling metrics (`container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total`) — if high, remove/increase CPU limits.

references.title: Tim Hockin (Kubernetes SIG-Node) — talks on CPU limits

questions.scenario: Tu app tiene traffic pattern con spikes 10x durante horas peak. HPA con CPU threshold 70% no funciona: cuando spike llega, HPA tarda 2 minutos en scale out, y ya sufriste 5xx en ese tiempo.
questions.question: ¿Qué estrategias mejoran responsividad de scaling?

options.text: Custom metrics HPA (via Prometheus Adapter): scale on request queue depth, or SQS backlog, or app-specific metric más leading que CPU.
options.why: Correcto. CPU es lagging indicator — spike ya golpeó cuando CPU sube. Métricas más leading: request queue length, SQS backlog, database connection saturation. HPA v2 supports custom metrics via metrics.k8s.io or custom.metrics.k8s.io APIs. Prometheus Adapter (KEDA popular) permite scale on any Prometheus metric. Ejemplo: scale workers based on SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessages.

options.text: Predictive scaling: schedule-based (KEDA CronScaler) pre-scale antes de horas peak conocidas.
options.why: Correcto. Si patrón es predictable (business hours, evening streaming spike), scale proactively via schedule. KEDA CronScaler o custom controller pre-provisions capacity antes del spike. Complement to reactive scaling — reactive handles unexpected, predictive handles known patterns.

options.text: Configurar HPA behavior: reducir stabilizationWindowSeconds (default 300s scale-down) para faster response. Aumentar scale-up rate via 'policies'.
options.why: Correcto. HPA v2 behavior spec permite tuning: scaleUp policies (max % or pods per period), scaleDown similar. Default conservative (avoid flapping). Aggressive scale-up + slow scale-down often desired. Ej: scale up 100% or 4 pods every 15s (fast); scale down 10% every 60s (gradual, avoid oscillation).

options.text: Cluster Autoscaler pre-provisioning nodes.
options.why: Correcto. HPA can request pods; if no nodes available, pods pending. Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes reactively (2-3 min in cloud). Solutions: (a) Overprovisioning nodes con placeholder low-priority pods (evicted on demand). (b) Karpenter (AWS) fast node provisioning. (c) Pre-warmed node pools. Enables HPA to actually scale quickly.

options.text: Aumentar CPU threshold a 90% para más 'headroom'.
options.why: Inverso: higher threshold = LATER scale-out = worse response. Lower threshold = earlier scale-out. Trade-off with cost (over-provision). No es la solución al slow response.

questions.explanation: Autoscaling responsiveness challenges: (1) HPA reactive: reacts to metric threshold crossed. Delay: metric collection window (15-60s) + HPA reconcile loop (15s) + pod startup (10s to minutes). Total: minutes typical for full scale-up. (2) Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes reactively (~2-3 min in cloud). Trade-offs: (a) Speed vs cost — over-provisioning wastes money, under-provisioning drops requests. (b) Metrics latency — CPU delayed, custom metrics can be earlier. (c) Pod startup time — image pull, init containers slow down scale-out. Solutions: (1) Pre-scaling — schedule-based (KEDA CronScaler) or forecast-based. (2) Custom metrics — leading indicators (queue depth, request rate). Prometheus Adapter or KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) simplify. (3) HPA v2 behavior — tune scale-up aggressive, scale-down gradual. (4) Overprovisioning — placeholder low-priority pods reserving nodes; evicted for real pods on demand. (5) Karpenter — AWS-native, faster than Cluster Autoscaler. (6) Warm pools — pre-created nodes. Cost of speed. Well-tuned HPA + Cluster Autoscaler + optionally KEDA + Karpenter can achieve sub-minute scale-out.
questions.realWorld: KEDA is CNCF project widely adopted for event-driven scaling (SQS, Kafka lag, Redis lists, cron). Karpenter (AWS 2021+) revolucionó Cluster Autoscaler with faster provisioning. Airbnb built custom autoscaling for their scale. Streaming services (Netflix, YouTube) use predictive + reactive combo. E-commerce during flash sales rely heavily on pre-scaling.

questions.scenario: Cluster de producción tiene node utilization promedio 25%. FinOps reporta $50k/mes en compute. Team defensivo: 'necesitamos capacity para picos'.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son estrategias para reducir costo sin sacrificar HA?

options.text: Bin packing más agresivo: aumentar Node density (más pods per node) con smaller nodes count. Requiere requests accurately sized. Karpenter/Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) ayudan.
options.why: Correcto. 25% utilization = 75% waste. Causas típicas: overprovisioned requests, sub-optimal bin packing, few large nodes with idle capacity. Solutions: (a) Right-size requests based on actual usage (VPA recommends). (b) Use bin-packing scheduler settings. (c) Karpenter smart node selection. (d) Consolidate to fewer larger nodes o larger workload density.

options.text: Spot/Preemptible instances para workloads fault-tolerant (batch, stateless web behind LB, dev): 50-90% cost reduction. Requires apps handle graceful shutdown (SIGTERM).
options.why: Correcto. Spot instances (AWS EC2 Spot, GCP Preemptible, Azure Spot) drastically cheaper (50-90% off). Trade-off: cloud reclaims with 2-min notice (varies). Suitable for: stateless workloads with quick startup, batch jobs, dev/test, distributed systems tolerating node loss (Cassandra, Spark). Not for: DBs single-node critical, stateful long-startup. Karpenter/AWS integrates spot smart. Mix on-demand (baseline) + spot (burst).

options.text: Autoscale nodes to actual demand (Cluster Autoscaler o Karpenter). Elimina fixed over-provisioning; nodes scale up/down con workload.
options.why: Correcto. Static node pool con capacity para peak = idle most of time. Dynamic scaling (Cluster Autoscaler removes underutilized nodes; adds nodes when pending pods). Karpenter more aggressive/faster. Adjusts to actual demand, not planned max. Combined with HPA para full-stack scaling.

options.text: Requests reduce sin límite basado en observado — VPA recommender.
options.why: Correcto (con caveat). VPA analiza usage histórico y recomienda requests. Common finding: requests over-set by 3-5x. Right-sizing improves bin-packing directly. Caveat: VPA restart pods to apply new requests (disruption); consider VPA off-mode (recommend only) + manual apply. Datadog, Grafana Cloud Cost analyze similar.

options.text: Reducir replicas por deployment a mínimo absoluto.
options.why: Sacrifica HA. Reducir de 3 → 1 replica ahorra pero un pod muerto = downtime. Compromise pobre. Right-size requests y usar autoscaling es better path que reducir replicas.

questions.explanation: Kubernetes cost optimization is significant discipline (FinOps). Common issues: (1) Over-provisioned requests — teams set requests defensively 5-10x actual usage. Wastes capacity. (2) Static nodes — fixed pool sized for peak, idle rest of time. (3) On-demand only — 3-5x cost vs spot alternatives. (4) Poor bin packing — many small pods on large nodes wasting. Solutions: (a) Right-sizing requests — VPA recommender, cost analytics tools (Kubecost, Datadog). Common savings 30-50%. (b) Cluster autoscaling — Cluster Autoscaler (traditional), Karpenter (AWS, faster/smarter). (c) Spot instances — for suitable workloads, 50-90% savings. Karpenter integrates. (d) Reserved instances / Savings Plans for baseline. (e) Node consolidation — fewer larger nodes better for bin packing typically. (f) Multi-tenancy — sharing nodes across teams (with resource quotas). (g) Kubecost, Cast.ai, Karpenter for AI cost optimization. Cost visibility: showback (team X used $Y this month) drives right behavior. Culture: engineers need to see cost impact of their choices.
questions.realWorld: Airbnb, Spotify publican FinOps journeys. Kubecost measures per-namespace/deployment cost. Cast.ai auto-optimizes. Karpenter (AWS 2021+) revolucionó node provisioning. Common finding: 30-50% cost savings possible with basic right-sizing. Uber famously reduces costs continuously. FinOps Foundation formaliza discipline.

questions.scenario: Team debate: para un backend API con traffic variable (0 requests at night, 10k/s durante día), ¿Kubernetes o Lambda?
questions.question: ¿Cuál es el análisis correcto?

options.text: Kubernetes siempre — es más flexible.
options.why: Simplistic. Kubernetes has fixed operational overhead: control plane cost, autoscaling latency, cold start of new nodes. For workload sitting idle at night, wastes capacity. Not always the answer.

options.text: Lambda siempre — es más simple.
options.why: Lambda has trade-offs: (a) Cold starts (100ms-seconds first invoke). (b) 15-min execution limit. (c) Cost at high sustained throughput can exceed EC2/K8s. (d) Runtime constraints (specific languages, image sizes). Not always cheapest at scale.

options.text: Depende del pattern: Lambda ideal for spiky/low-throughput workloads (paga solo por invocación, escala a zero). Kubernetes better for sustained/predictable throughput (idle cost of K8s > Lambda per-invoke; sustained cost of Lambda > K8s). Crossover typically around 100-1000 rps sustained. También Lambda para event-driven (S3 triggers, Cognito hooks), Kubernetes for long-running services or complex apps.
options.why: Correcto y matizado. Analysis based on cost + performance profile. Lambda: pay-per-invocation (~$0.20 per 1M requests + compute time). Great for spiky workloads o event handlers. Bad for high sustained load (calculate: 10k rps * 60s * 60min * 24h * 30d = 25B invocations/mo = $5k just per-invoke, plus compute). Kubernetes: fixed cost (nodes running 24/7) + variable (autoscale). Better ROI at sustained scale. Crossover point varies but often ~100-1000 rps sustained. Mixed strategy: Kubernetes for baseline, Lambda for spikes/events común.

options.text: Ambos son equivalentes; elegir por preferencia del equipo.
options.why: Real trade-offs exist (cost, latency, complexity). Preference matters but data should drive decision. 'Preference' as sole criterion leads to expensive mistakes.

questions.explanation: Serverless (Lambda, Cloud Functions, Azure Functions) vs Container orchestration (Kubernetes, ECS): (1) Serverless: pay-per-invocation, scales to zero, no infra management. Great for: event-driven, spiky, low-throughput, quick startup requirements. Limitations: cold starts, execution time limits, memory/storage limits, runtime constraints. (2) Kubernetes: pay-for-nodes, always-on (unless scaled down), full flexibility. Great for: sustained throughput, long-running processes, complex apps, stateful services. Overhead: control plane cost, ops complexity. Cost analysis: (a) Low volume (<1k rps sustained): Lambda usually cheaper. (b) High sustained volume: Kubernetes/EC2 cheaper. Crossover depends on workload characteristics. (c) Spiky (0 to peak): Lambda's scale-to-zero saves at trough. (d) Event-driven (S3 triggers, DynamoDB streams): Lambda idiomatic. Mixed architecture common: (a) Kubernetes for core APIs. (b) Lambda for event handlers, low-volume endpoints. (c) Fargate (AWS) for container serverless — bridges gap. (d) Cloud Run (GCP) similar. Considerations: (a) Cold start SLA — first request slow with Lambda unless provisioned concurrency. (b) Deployment simplicity — Lambda deploy = upload zip. K8s deploy = complex. (c) Team skills — Lambda simpler for small teams. Kubernetes overhead needs SRE.
questions.realWorld: Netflix uses Kubernetes for streaming service, Lambda for event triggers. Coca-Cola migrated some to Lambda for cost. Segment moved from microservicios back to monolith (published case study). Startups often start Lambda-first (rapid iteration), migrate to K8s as scale. Enterprise usually mixed. AWS Fargate y Google Cloud Run offer middle ground (serverless containers).

questions.scenario: Deployment de 10 replicas. Deploy nueva versión que tiene bug (crashea al arrancar). Team desea que solo pocos pods sean afectados para debugging antes de rollback.
questions.question: ¿Qué configuración de Rolling Update ayuda?

options.text: maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0: crear 1 pod nuevo a la vez, no matar viejos hasta que nuevo ready. Si nuevo pod falla readiness probe, deployment pausa (no progresa). Solo 1 pod nuevo (dañado) mientras 10 antiguos sirven. Fácil rollback.
options.why: Correcto para pattern conservador. maxSurge=1 permite 1 extra pod (total 11) during rollout; maxUnavailable=0 means never below 10 healthy. Deployment adds new pod, waits for ready, if ready → mata 1 antiguo, adds next. Si new pod nunca ready (bug crashes it), deployment queda stuck en 11 pods (10 old + 1 new failing) — team ve problema, rollback rápido. Readiness probes CRÍTICAS para este pattern funcionar (sin ellas, K8s pensaría el pod nuevo está OK cuando en realidad es bug).

options.text: maxSurge=50%, maxUnavailable=50%: rollout rápido.
options.why: Rollout rápido, pero problema: 50% de traffic va a pods potencialmente broken durante rollout. Si new version es bad, 50% de users sufren. Menos conservador, más riesgo. Aceptable si high confidence en rollout (auto tests exhaustive).

options.text: Recreate strategy: mata todos los pods old, luego crea new.
options.why: Recreate = downtime durante rollout. Todos old muertos antes de crear new. Sin traffic durante window. Aceptable solo si downtime OK (dev env, workloads que require single version at time como certain DB migrations).

options.text: Sin especificar, K8s eligirá strategy correcta.
options.why: Default RollingUpdate uses maxSurge=25%, maxUnavailable=25%. Puede afectar 25% traffic durante rollout — no ideal para this scenario. Elegir explicitly para safety.

questions.explanation: Deployment rollout strategies: (1) RollingUpdate (default) — gradual replacement. Config: maxSurge (extra pods during rollout), maxUnavailable (below desired during rollout). Conservative: maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0. Aggressive: maxSurge=100%, maxUnavailable=0 (double capacity temporarily). (2) Recreate — kill all, then create new. Downtime. For legacy apps or single-version-at-time semantics. (3) Blue-Green (not native, via services) — deploy new full copy, switch service selector. Rapid rollback (switch back). More resources temporarily. (4) Canary (not native, via Argo Rollouts, Flagger) — small % traffic to new version, monitor, gradually shift. (5) A/B testing — traffic split by header/cookie/user segment. Readiness probes ESSENCIAL: (a) Without readiness, Kubernetes considers pod ready as soon as container starts — routing traffic to broken pod. (b) With readiness (HTTP GET, TCP, exec), pod not receiving traffic until probe passes. Deploy pause on failing readiness. (c) Consider startupProbe (K8s 1.16+) for slow-start apps que confuse readiness. Combined with monitoring/alerts on rollout (Argo Rollouts + Flagger integration with Prometheus/Datadog for auto-rollback on SLI regression), safer deployments.
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes native rolling update is basic. Production teams use Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker for advanced patterns (canary, blue-green, progressive delivery). Netflix Spinnaker pioneered many patterns. Argo Rollouts + Prometheus enables auto-rollback on SLI breach. Full continuous deployment requires more than plain Deployment. FluxCD, ArgoCD popular for GitOps deployment.

questions.scenario: Platform team hosts 20+ product teams en un shared Kubernetes cluster. Consideraciones: aislamiento, quotas, security, self-service.
questions.question: ¿Qué mecanismos combinar para multi-tenancy safe?

options.text: Namespaces per team: soft aislamiento vía Kubernetes namespaces. RBAC restringe team X a modificar solo su namespace.
options.why: Correcto y foundation. Namespaces son unit de organización en K8s. RBAC (Role, RoleBinding, ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding) permite grant/deny específico. Cada team ownership de su namespace. Baseline multi-tenancy. Note: namespace es LOGICAL boundary, NO security boundary por sí solo (pods can talk across namespaces default; escapes possible via kernel bugs).

options.text: ResourceQuota + LimitRange: cap resources per namespace (evitar noisy neighbor).
options.why: Correcto. ResourceQuota caps total (namespace can use max N CPU, M memory, P pods). LimitRange sets defaults + max per pod/container. Prevents one team consuming entire cluster. Essential for fair sharing. Combine with priority classes para preemption cuando cluster saturado.

options.text: NetworkPolicy: default-deny + explicit allow entre namespaces. Restringe network access between tenants.
options.why: Correcto. Sin NetworkPolicy, todos los pods can talk to todos (flat network). NetworkPolicy (implemented by CNI: Calico, Cilium, Weave) enforces L3/L4 rules. Common pattern: default-deny + allow ingress from specific namespaces. Complement con service mesh (mTLS + L7 authz) for stronger isolation.

options.text: PodSecurityStandards (o admission controllers custom): enforce security policies (no root, no privileged, no hostNetwork).
options.why: Correcto. PodSecurityStandards (K8s 1.25+, replaced PSP) has 3 levels: Privileged, Baseline, Restricted. Restricted en tenant namespaces prevents root, privileged, hostPath, etc. — reduces blast radius. Custom admission controllers (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper) enable custom policies (must have labels, image from approved registry, etc.). Essential for compliance/security.

options.text: Dar cluster-admin a cada team.
options.why: Anti-tenancy. cluster-admin = full cluster access = can modify others' resources, delete namespaces, escalate. Multi-tenancy requires PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE — restrict to needed resources only.

questions.explanation: Kubernetes multi-tenancy levels: (1) Soft multi-tenancy — internal teams trust-based. Namespaces + RBAC + Quotas + NetworkPolicy. Kubernetes default assumption. (2) Hard multi-tenancy — external tenants, adversarial assumption. Requires stronger isolation: separate clusters (vCluster, KaaS), gVisor/Kata Containers for kernel isolation, strict admission. Kubernetes native isn't designed for hard multi-tenancy — kernel is shared. Components: (a) Namespaces — logical grouping, RBAC scope. (b) RBAC — Role/ClusterRole + RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding. Deny by default with grants. (c) ResourceQuota — cap resources per namespace. LimitRange — per-pod defaults/max. (d) NetworkPolicy — L3/L4 firewall between pods. Default-deny + explicit allow. (e) PodSecurityStandards — pod security constraints (no root, no privileged). (f) Admission controllers — policy engines (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper) for custom policies. (g) Service accounts — pod identity, scoped per namespace. (h) Secret management — sealed-secrets, external secrets operator, Vault integration. (i) Cost allocation — Kubecost per-namespace. Advanced: (a) Virtual clusters (vCluster) — nested control plane per tenant. (b) Sandbox runtimes (gVisor, Kata) — additional kernel isolation. (c) Dedicated node pools per tenant.
questions.realWorld: GKE, EKS, AKS provide managed multi-tenancy features. Airbnb famously uses multi-tenant K8s clusters. Uber has multi-tenant platform. Netflix similar. Startups often start single-tenant per cluster, migrate to shared as ops team scales. SaaS companies use shared clusters for customer isolation with careful controls (Snyk, Datadog, etc.).

questions.scenario: Team implementa new APIs en K8s. Debate: ¿usar Ingress o el nuevo Gateway API?
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la diferencia y cuál elegir en 2026?

options.text: Ingress (legacy): HTTP-focused, limited features (routing por host/path). Annotations vendor-specific hackear features avanzados. Un solo Ingress resource controlado por Ingress Controller (Nginx, Traefik, HAProxy). Gateway API (2023 GA): standardized, extensible, multi-protocol (HTTP, TCP, UDP), multi-team ownership (Gateway per team, HTTPRoute per app), first-class support for advanced routing (headers, methods, weighted). CNCF community moving toward Gateway API. New deployments should evaluate Gateway API; existing Ingress remains functional.
options.why: Correcto. Ingress limitations: (a) Only HTTP L7, no TCP/UDP. (b) Basic routing (host + path). (c) Advanced features (rewrites, canary, headers) via vendor annotations — non-portable. (d) Single Ingress resource per zone often mixes team concerns. Gateway API: (a) Multi-protocol. (b) Standard routing spec (HTTPRoute, TCPRoute, GRPCRoute, TLSRoute). (c) Role separation: Infrastructure Provider (GatewayClass), Cluster Operator (Gateway), Application Developer (HTTPRoute). (d) Extensible via policy attachments. (e) Cross-namespace routing. Implementations: Istio, Contour, Envoy Gateway, Linkerd, cloud provider load balancers. 2023 GA milestone. 2024-2026 recommended for new deployments; existing Ingress remains supported.

options.text: Ingress siempre — es más estable.
options.why: Ingress limita crecimiento. Gateway API es nueva pero GA and stable, adopted by major implementations. Nuevo work debería considerar Gateway API.

options.text: Gateway API siempre — Ingress deprecated.
options.why: Ingress NO deprecated. Coexisten. Migration is opt-in, no forced. Muchos deployments existentes seguirán con Ingress. Elección informada por needs.

options.text: Son idénticos, solo diferentes nombres.
options.why: Diferencias sustanciales (spec, capabilities, ownership model). Diseñados con distintos objetivos. Gateway API is not 'Ingress v2 rename'.

questions.explanation: Gateway API evolution: Ingress API (2015+) resolved 'how to route external traffic to K8s services' pero limitations became apparent: HTTP only, vendor annotations for advanced features, single resource conflates infrastructure/routing concerns. Gateway API (SIG Network 2020-2023): (1) Roles separation — GatewayClass (infra type), Gateway (deployment), HTTPRoute (routing rules). (2) Multi-protocol — HTTPRoute, TCPRoute, GRPCRoute, TLSRoute. (3) Advanced routing — header-based, method-based, weighted (canary), timeouts. (4) Cross-namespace — Route in namespace A can attach to Gateway in namespace B (con permissions). (5) Extensibility — Policy attachments (rate limit, retry, auth) via CRDs. (6) Portable — no vendor annotations. Implementations 2026: Istio, Contour (VMware), Envoy Gateway (CNCF), Linkerd, GKE Gateway, Traefik, HAProxy, NGINX Kubernetes Gateway, Cilium. Migration: no urgency; Ingress supported. Gateway API benefits accrue over time (better mental model, portability, advanced features). New projects strongly considered.
questions.realWorld: GKE Gateway (Google managed), Azure Application Gateway for Containers, Contour production. Envoy Gateway CNCF project 2022+. Istio Gateway (their pre-Gateway-API resource, similar concept). Kubernetes SIG-Network active. Adoption growing 2024-2026. Ingress still dominant install base pero Gateway API is future.

questions.scenario: Team desplega manually con kubectl apply. Auditoría requiere: quién cambió qué, cuándo, why. Rollback confuso, environments drift entre staging/prod.
questions.question: ¿Qué patrón resuelve estos problemas?

options.text: GitOps: git repo es SOURCE OF TRUTH de desired state cluster. Herramientas (ArgoCD, Flux) sync git → cluster continuously. Cambios via PR (audit, review, approval). Rollback = git revert. Environments drift eliminated (source es git, no manual). Beneficios: auditoría automática, rollback rápido, DR (rebuild cluster from git), consistency multi-env.
options.why: Correcto. GitOps (Weaveworks 2017 term) es approach cloud-native: (1) Git repo describes desired state (Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, Kustomize overlays). (2) Controller (ArgoCD, Flux) continuamente compara git vs cluster, applies changes. (3) Cambios via git commit/PR (review, audit, approve). (4) Rollback = git revert previous commit. (5) DR: recreate cluster from git without human intervention. Enables safer, more reliable, more auditable ops. CNCF projects: ArgoCD (Intuit), Flux (Weaveworks/CNCF).

options.text: Migrar a serverless para evitar el problema.
options.why: No resuelve — serverless también needs deployment pipeline con audit. Además cambio de arquitectura mayor por resolver process issue. GitOps es lightweight y aplicable a Kubernetes.

options.text: Setup CI/CD que hace kubectl apply on merge.
options.why: Half-solution. CI pipeline puede aplicar cambios pero: (a) drift NOT detected (manual changes con kubectl persist), (b) no continuous reconciliation (only on trigger), (c) rollback requires re-running pipeline. GitOps controller continuously reconciles, detecting/reverting drift automatically.

options.text: Documentar cambios en wiki para audit.
options.why: Manual, error-prone, not automated. Audit is by-product of GitOps naturally. Wiki es process patch que no escala.

questions.explanation: GitOps principles (OpenGitOps standard): (1) Declarative — desired state described declaratively (K8s manifests). (2) Versioned + immutable — git is source of truth, versioned history. (3) Pulled automatically — controller in cluster pulls (not pushed from CI). (4) Continuously reconciled — controller detects drift, applies desired state continuously. Tools: (a) ArgoCD — CD platform, UI-friendly, hierarchical Application concept, multi-cluster. (b) Flux — CLI-friendly, GitOps toolkit modular components (source, kustomize, helm, notification controllers). (c) Jenkins X, Fleet, others. Patterns: (a) App-of-apps (ArgoCD) or Kustomizations (Flux) for managing many apps. (b) Environments via git branches or directories. (c) Secrets: sealed-secrets or external-secrets-operator (don't commit plaintext secrets). (d) Progressive delivery: ArgoCD Rollouts, Flagger. Benefits realized: audit trail (git log), rollback (git revert), DR (bootstrap from git), consistency (no manual kubectl). Real transformation of Kubernetes ops practice.
questions.realWorld: Weaveworks pioneered GitOps 2017. Intuit created ArgoCD, donated to CNCF. Flux graduated CNCF. Microsoft, Google, AWS integrate GitOps into managed K8s. Codefresh, Akuity commercial. Almost every serious K8s deployment uses ArgoCD or Flux (or roll-your-own). Practices at scale: Airbnb, Adobe, Zoom.

questions.scenario: Cluster Kubernetes con Istio sufre latency por Envoy sidecars (~1-2ms per hop x N hops). Team evalúa alternativas.
questions.question: ¿Qué tecnología emergente aborda esto?

options.text: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter): kernel-level programmability. Cilium (CNI + service mesh) implementa policies + observability en kernel (bypass userspace hops). Sidecar-less alternative to Istio. Better performance (no extra userspace hop), less resource overhead. Ambient Mesh (Istio 2023+) también reduces sidecar per-pod.
options.why: Correcto. eBPF es tecnología revolucionaria — safely run programs in Linux kernel (via VM + verifier). Applications: networking (Cilium replaces iptables/IPVS), observability (Falco, Pixie), security (runtime protection). Cilium: CNI + service mesh built on eBPF. Advantages over sidecar mesh: (a) Faster (kernel-level packet processing vs userspace). (b) Less memory (no Envoy per pod, ~50MB/pod savings x 1000 pods = 50GB). (c) L7 policies in kernel. Trade-offs: (a) Newer tech, less mature ecosystem. (b) Kernel version requirements. (c) Complex debugging. Ambient Mesh (Istio) es alternative approach: shared per-node ztunnel + waypoint proxies as needed. Both reducing sidecar overhead concern.

options.text: Increase Envoy resources.
options.why: Doesn't address structural overhead — sidecar per pod remains. Alternatives fundamentally rearchitect.

options.text: Remove service mesh entirely.
options.why: Loses features (mTLS, retries, observability). Alternatives (eBPF-based mesh) provide features with less overhead.

options.text: Bare metal only.
options.why: Not related — mesh overhead exists on any infra. Bare metal doesn't solve service-to-service communication overhead.

questions.explanation: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter, evolved from packet filtering) enables safe programmability of Linux kernel. Programs written in restricted C, verified for safety, JIT-compiled. Use cases: (1) Networking — replace iptables/IPVS (which don't scale to 1000s of services well). Cilium uses eBPF for L3/L4/L7 policies, load balancing. (2) Observability — trace syscalls, network flows, function calls without instrumentation (Pixie, Parca). (3) Security — runtime monitoring, attack detection (Falco, Tetragon). (4) Performance — replace kernel routines for specific workloads. Cilium: CNI (network plugin) + service mesh + observability + security in one, powered by eBPF. Sidecar-less mesh: policies in kernel, no per-pod Envoy. Impact: (a) Latency reduction (~500us saved per hop typical). (b) Resource savings (memory, CPU). (c) Better observability (kernel visibility). Trade-offs: (a) Kernel version dependency (eBPF features evolve). (b) Complex to debug/develop. (c) Ecosystem younger than iptables-based. Industry direction: Cilium (CNCF graduated 2023) adopted increasingly. Ambient Mesh (Istio 2023+) parallel effort reducing sidecar overhead differently. Isovalent (Cilium's company) acquired by Cisco 2023.
questions.realWorld: Google GKE Dataplane V2 usa Cilium. AWS EKS + Cilium option. Netflix uses eBPF for observability. Datadog Live Container view uses eBPF. Sysdig for security. eBPF Summit, Cilium Community growing. 2024-2026 seeing broad adoption. LinkedIn moving to Cilium. Cost/perf gains at scale justify migration.

questions.scenario: Cluster upgrade evicts pods for node drains. Sin config, all replicas de un deployment critical se pueden mover simultaneously → downtime.
questions.question: ¿Qué feature previene esto?

options.text: PodDisruptionBudget (PDB): declara mínimo pods disponibles o máximo unavailable durante VOLUNTARY disruptions (node drain, cluster upgrades). eviction API respeta PDB. Ejemplo: minAvailable: 2 en deployment de 3 replicas = solo 1 puede ser evicted at a time.
options.why: Correcto. PDB (Pod Disruption Budget) es mecanismo declarativo para safety durante voluntary disruptions (node drain, upgrade, cluster autoscaler downscale, admin operations). API eviction () consulta PDB antes de evict — if would violate, blocked (wait or reject). Fields: minAvailable (min pods must stay) or maxUnavailable (max can be down). Applies solo a VOLUNTARY disruptions — no INVOLUNTARY (node crash, hardware failure). Complementa readiness probes + replicaSet ensuring availability during operations.

options.text: Replica count alto — set 10 replicas para HA.
options.why: Ayuda pero no controla eviction rate. Sin PDB, cluster upgrade puede evict 10 replicas simultaneously si K8s policy allows. PDB caps concurrent evictions.

options.text: priorityClass alto.
options.why: priorityClass controls preemption y eviction priority en resource pressure. Diferente concern. PDB específicamente para voluntary disruption control.

options.text: K8s automáticamente respeta HA.
options.why: Kubernetes por default NO enforces distribución specific de disruptions. kubectl drain honors PDB solo si specified. Sin PDB, node drain acepta evicting all pods en el node simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Pod Disruption Budget: declara constraints en concurrent voluntary disruptions. Spec: `minAvailable: N` or `maxUnavailable: N or %`. Applies to pods matching selector (usually same as deployment). Voluntary disruptions include: (a) Node drain (kubectl drain, cordon+drain for maintenance). (b) Cluster autoscaler downscaling. (c) Rolling updates (indirectly, via deployment strategy). (d) Admin evictions. Involuntary (NOT PDB-covered): (a) Node kernel panic. (b) VM instance deleted by cloud. (c) Hardware failure. Rely on replicas + monitoring for these. Common configs: (a) Web tier 3 replicas: PDB minAvailable=2. Only 1 can be evicted at a time. (b) DB cluster with quorum: PDB ensures quorum preservation during drain. (c) Zero-downtime services: maxUnavailable=0 (careful — can block cluster upgrades entirely if pods hard to reschedule). Considerations: (a) PDB with all replicas on one node → eviction blocked. Combine with anti-affinity for spread. (b) PDB too strict blocks legitimate operations. (c) Cluster autoscaler respects PDB (won't scale down node if would violate). Kubernetes ecosystem: cluster autoscaler, Karpenter, kubectl drain all honor PDB.
questions.realWorld: Every serious production K8s deployment has PDBs. Node maintenance during cloud provider upgrades relies on PDB for safe drain. Autoscaler downscaling uses PDB awareness. Missing PDB = production incidents during ops. Kubernetes upgrades themselves rely on this. Managed K8s (GKE, EKS, AKS) auto-handle upgrades honoring PDBs.

questions.scenario: Cluster con 5000 pods, cada uno con Envoy sidecar (~100MB memory, 0.1 CPU). Total overhead: 500GB memory, 500 CPU cores just for sidecars. FinOps upset.
questions.question: ¿Qué soluciones existen para reducir sidecar overhead en escala grande?

options.text: Aumentar nodes size — más capacity total.
options.why: No resuelve — sigue pagando overhead per pod. Solo esconde el costo en mayor node bill. Overhead structural remains.

options.text: Ambient Mesh (Istio 2023+): eliminate per-pod sidecar. Per-node ztunnel handles L4 + mTLS; waypoint proxy per namespace/service para L7 (optional). Dramatic reduction en per-pod overhead. Alternatively Cilium Service Mesh (eBPF-based sidecar-less). Trade-offs: newer tech, operational complexity distinct.
options.why: Correcto. Ambient Mesh (Istio) diseñado específicamente para reducir sidecar overhead: (1) ztunnel — DaemonSet per node handling L4 + mTLS. Shared across all pods on node. (2) Waypoint proxy — optional per-namespace/service Envoy for L7 features (only where needed). Result: baseline mTLS with minimal overhead; L7 selectively. Cilium Service Mesh: eBPF-based, kernel handles most functions, no per-pod sidecar. Both approaches emerged 2022-2023 responding to sidecar overhead concerns. Trade-offs: different operational model, ecosystem maturing.

options.text: Remove service mesh entirely.
options.why: Loses mTLS, retries, observability. If value was there, removing loses features. Alternative approaches preserve features with lower overhead.

options.text: Larger Envoy sidecars — 200MB each is fine.
options.why: Opuesto del problema. Aumentaría cost, no reduce.

questions.explanation: Sidecar overhead at scale: 5000 pods × 100MB Envoy = 500GB just for mesh proxies. Substantial cost. Solutions: (1) Ambient Mesh (Istio 2023+): (a) ztunnel — per-node DaemonSet, one shared instance vs one per pod. (b) Handles L4 encryption (mTLS), routing, metrics. (c) Waypoint proxy — optional per-namespace or per-service Envoy for advanced L7 (headers, retries, weighted routing). Deployed only where needed. (d) Reduces baseline overhead significantly, L7 selective. (2) Cilium Service Mesh: eBPF-based, kernel handles service mesh functions. Sidecar-less by design. (3) Optimize sidecar config — smaller Envoy config (only necessary filters), tighter resource limits. Optimizations only, not structural. (4) Selective mesh — only apply to critical services, not everything. Considerations: (a) Migration to ambient/Cilium is significant undertaking. (b) Ecosystem maturity — sidecar mesh has years of production. Newer approaches evolving. (c) Debugging model different (harder in some ways, easier in others). (d) Feature parity — ambient/Cilium may lack some advanced features initially. At mega-scale (Google, Netflix), custom solutions or heavy investment in ambient/Cilium. Mid-scale might stay with sidecars accepting overhead.
questions.realWorld: Solo IO (Istio maintainers) actively developing Ambient Mesh. Isovalent (Cilium) acquired by Cisco 2023 — massive investment. Google Anthos supports ambient. Uber, Airbnb evaluated ambient. LinkedIn migrating to Cilium reports significant savings. Trade-off decisions being made in industry now.

questions.scenario: Team new a Kubernetes commits varios anti-patterns. Como senior, identificas.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles de estos son anti-patterns? (marca todos)

options.text: Latest image tag en producción.
options.why: Correcto. `image: myapp:latest` = non-deterministic. Kubernetes cache images per node; new pods may pull different content bajo same 'latest' tag. Also breaks GitOps (git says 'latest', cluster has version X, no reconciliation possible). Use immutable tags (git SHA, semver, timestamp). Also set imagePullPolicy: Always con specific tag to ensure freshness.

options.text: kubectl exec para debugging producción.
options.why: Correcto con matiz. kubectl exec into production pod → change goes untracked, mutable pod state, breaks immutability principle. Además privileged access risks. Preferable: (a) Debug via logs/metrics/traces first. (b) Attach ephemeral debug container (K8s 1.25+). (c) Reproduce issue in staging. (d) SSH sesiones auditadas. Ocasional debugging OK but should not be normal ops.

options.text: Storing secrets as plain Kubernetes Secrets in git.
options.why: Correcto. Kubernetes Secret objects are base64-encoded (NO encrypted) by default in etcd. Committing to git exposes them. Solutions: (a) Sealed Secrets (Bitnami) — encrypt in git, decrypt in cluster. (b) External Secrets Operator — sync from Vault/AWS SM/GCP SM. (c) SOPS + git — encrypt with age/GPG. (d) etcd encryption at rest para Secrets protection. Plain Secrets in git es leak waiting to happen.

options.text: Running as root in containers.
options.why: Correcto. Container escape vulnerabilities more dangerous con root. Set runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000 (or specific non-root UID). PodSecurityStandards 'Restricted' enforces. Rebuilding images not-as-root can be one-time work but critical hardening.

options.text: Configuring resources requests based on actual observed usage.
options.why: Esto es GOOD PRACTICE (right-sizing), not anti-pattern. VPA / analysis tools recommend requests based on data. Improves bin packing y cost.

questions.explanation: Common K8s anti-patterns (SIG-Security, best practices docs): (1) Latest image tag — non-deterministic deploys. Use immutable tags. (2) No resource limits/requests — noisy neighbor, OOM cascades. Set appropriate. (3) Root containers — escape risk, unnecessary privilege. Non-root user. (4) Privileged containers — kernel access. Only if truly needed. (5) hostNetwork / hostPID / hostIPC — bypasses container isolation. (6) HostPath volumes — writes to node filesystem. Data loss on pod move, security risk. (7) No liveness/readiness probes — Kubernetes can't detect issues. (8) Long-running init containers — slow pod startup. (9) Untagged images / vulnerabilities — scan with Trivy, Snyk. (10) Broad RBAC (cluster-admin to service accounts) — least privilege. (11) No NetworkPolicy — flat network. (12) Secrets as plain env vars in git manifests — leaks. Use secrets manager integration. (13) kubectl exec / manual changes in prod — breaks GitOps, unauditable. (14) Ignoring events (kubectl get events) — misses issues. (15) All namespaces default — no isolation. Combining these reduces reliability, security, cost efficiency. Enforcement via admission controllers (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno).
questions.realWorld: Every K8s security audit finds subset of these. NSA/CISA published Kubernetes Hardening Guide covering these. CNCF Security TAG maintains best practices. Kubernetes conformance tests enforce some. Tools (Datree, Kubescape, Polaris) audit configurations. Cultural adoption of best practices takes time.

questions.scenario: Startup de 3 developers necesita hostear su app monolítica (Rails + Postgres). CTO propone Kubernetes 'para estar cloud-native'.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la respuesta correcta?

options.text: Kubernetes siempre — es el standard.
options.why: Antipattern común. K8s tiene operational overhead (upgrades, security patches, autoscaler tuning, network debugging). Para 3 devs con 1 app, overhead > value. Managed services (Heroku, Fly.io, Railway, App Engine, Elastic Beanstalk, Cloud Run) proporcionan cloud-native benefits sin K8s complexity.

options.text: Depende del context: para startup pequeño con app simple, alternatives más pragmáticas: (1) Managed PaaS (Heroku, Fly.io, Railway, Render) — deploy con git push, cero infra management. (2) Serverless containers (AWS Fargate, Cloud Run) — no K8s cluster manage. (3) VPS con Docker Compose. Reservar K8s para cuando (a) equipo tiene skills K8s, (b) escala/complexity justifican operational overhead, (c) necesitas features específicas (advanced scheduling, custom controllers). Regla: usa la herramienta más simple que satisface requirements, not la más 'moderna'.
options.why: Correcto. Kubernetes NO es free lunch. Ops complexity real: cluster upgrades trimestral, control plane maintenance, network debugging, security patching, autoscaler tuning, RBAC management. Requires dedicated SRE mindset. Para monolithic app + small team, this is disproportionate. Alternatives: (a) Heroku — deploy git push, managed everything, expensive at scale but zero ops. (b) Fly.io — modern PaaS, containers globally distributed. (c) Cloud Run/Fargate — serverless containers, scale-to-zero, no cluster. (d) VPS + Docker Compose — simple, cheap. Start with simpler; migrate to K8s when actually needed.

options.text: No — usar bare metal siempre.
options.why: Extremo opuesto. Bare metal es MÁS ops overhead que K8s (patching OS, backups, HW failures manually). Cloud/managed services often sweet spot for small teams.

options.text: Depende del budget: si tienen $ para managed K8s, sí; si no, Docker.
options.why: Budget importa pero no es factor primario. Skills, complexity, actual needs matter more. Managed K8s (GKE, EKS) reduce ops burden pero no eliminate — still need K8s expertise to use effectively.

questions.explanation: K8s decision framework: (1) Team size — small teams sin K8s skills → managed PaaS. K8s needs ~1+ SRE full-time to run well. (2) App complexity — monolith or few services → PaaS/simple. Microservicios many → K8s makes sense. (3) Scale — low traffic → PaaS/serverless. High traffic → K8s or dedicated infra. (4) Cloud lock-in preferences — K8s portable, managed services often lock-in. Alternatives to K8s: (a) Heroku, Render, Railway, Fly.io — full PaaS. Deploy git push. Managed everything. Expensive at scale, minimal ops. (b) AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine, Azure App Service — cloud PaaS. Similar. (c) AWS Fargate, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Instances — serverless containers. Pay per use. (d) VPS with Docker/Compose — simple, cheap, some ops. (e) Nomad (HashiCorp) — simpler orchestrator alternative to K8s. Rule: 'boring technology'. Choose simplest that works. K8s justified when: microservicios diverse, need advanced orchestration (custom controllers, complex scheduling), team has expertise. Otherwise, PaaS/serverless simpler.
questions.realWorld: DHH (Rails/Basecamp) famously anti-microservicios/K8s — 'Majestic Monolith'. GitHub scaled monolith massively. Stack Overflow ran on few servers. Fly.io, Render growing fast for small-medium teams. Vercel/Netlify dominate frontend hosting. K8s dominates large enterprise but small teams often better with PaaS. 'You are not Google' meme reminds us most orgs aren't at scale needing K8s.

references.title: OZ's — 'Why you probably don't need Kubernetes'
